claims.text: HEA coating wear resistance is primarily governed by the nanoindentation hardness-to-reduced-modulus ratio Hn/Er.
Increasing Hn/Er improves resistance to plastic deformation during wear.
Improved resistance to plastic deformation reduces wear volume.
Increased dislocation density and refined grain or sub-grain structures can raise coating hardness while leaving elastic modulus substantially unchanged.
Microstructural refinement can increase Hn/Er in HEA coatings.
AlCoCrxCuFe and NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 are representative as-deposited HEA coating systems for the proposed test.
Such HEA coatings are typically produced by methods including magnetron sputtering on stainless-steel substrates.
A heat treatment or ultrasonic-vibration treatment can selectively increase nanoindentation hardness without significantly changing elastic modulus.
A higher Hn/Er impedes the initiation and propagation of damage under repeated mechanical loading.
Impeded damage initiation and propagation reduce abrasive and adhesive wear.
Post-treated coatings with higher Hn/Er will have lower cumulative wear volume than untreated coatings.
Post-treated coatings with higher Hn/Er will have lower friction coefficients than untreated coatings.
Post-treated coatings with higher Hn/Er will exhibit more stable friction coefficients.
The proposed Hn/Er relationship should hold from room temperature to approximately 300 °C under dry-sliding or cavitation conditions.
Coatings with substantially different phase compositions may not follow the proposed Hn/Er–wear relationship.
The quantitative relationship between Hn/Er and wear-volume reduction varies among HEA systems.
Phase composition and residual stress can influence HEA coating wear performance independently of Hn/Er.
Adhesion-related effects can influence HEA coating wear performance.

contradictions.description: The experiment allows cavitation erosion as the selected test while requiring continuous coefficient-of-friction measurements and friction improvement as an outcome; coefficient of friction is not ordinarily defined for a cavitation-only test.
